ex.en: I live on Herzl Street.

note: Masculine, but the plural ends in -ot: רחובות (rekhovót). Note the preposition: ברחוב = on the street. Same root as רחב (wide).

ex.en: There's a bank near my house.

note: A branch is a סניף: הסניף של הבנק = the bank's branch.

ex.en: Excuse me, where's the post office?

note: Means both the mail and the post office; a branch is a סניף דואר. Email is formally דואר אלקטרוני, but everyone says מייל.

ex.en: On Saturday we have a picnic in the park.

note: A big park. A small neighbourhood park or playground is a גינה. פארק הירקון is Tel Aviv's biggest park.

ex.en: We're going to the playground with the kids.

note: A small neighbourhood park, usually with a playground (גינה ציבורית), or a private garden. גינת כלבים = dog park. Same root as גן (garden).

ex.he: יש בית כנסת קטן ברחוב שלנו.
ex.en: There's a small synagogue on our street.

note: Lit. "house of assembly" (root כ.נ.ס, to gather, as in the Knesset). With "the", the ה goes on the second word: בית הכנסת.

ex.en: There's a beautiful mosque in Jaffa.

note: From the root ס.ג.ד (to bow down), like the Arabic masjid.

ex.en: There are many churches in Nazareth.

note: Same root as בית כנסת and the Knesset (כ.נ.ס, to gather). Also spelled כנסיה.

ex.he: אבא של סמיר רופא בבית חולים.
ex.en: Samir's dad is a doctor at a hospital.

note: Lit. "house of the sick". With "the": בית החולים. The ER is חדר מיון.

ex.en: There's a new school in the neighbourhood.

note: Lit. "house of the book". With "the": בית הספר. Often abbreviated בי״ס.

ex.en: Our son is in kindergarten.

note: Usually just גן: היא בגן = she's at kindergarten (roughly ages 3–6). The teacher is the גננת.

ex.en: I borrow books from the library.

note: False friend: a library, not a bookshop (that's חנות ספרים). Also a bookcase at home. Same root as ספר (book).

ex.en: The museum is open on Saturday too.

note: Stress on the last syllable: muze'ón. מוזיאון ישראל in Jerusalem is the best known.

ex.en: It's a good, cheap restaurant.

note: Root ס.ע.ד (to dine). מסעדה כשרה = a kosher restaurant.

ex.he: אני פוגשת את יוליה בבית קפה.
ex.en: I'm meeting Yulia at a café.

note: With "the": בית הקפה. In compounds the plural of בית is בתי (batéi), not בתים.

ex.en: The restaurant is right by the junction.

note: Irregular plural צמתים (tsmatím). Most speakers treat it as masculine (הצומת הבא); feminine is also heard.

ex.en: At the second traffic light, turn right.

note: A modern blend of רמז (signal, hint) + אור (light). In directions, the impersonal plural פונים (lit. "one turns") is the normal way to say "turn".

ex.en: The bank? To the right, after the post office.

note: ימין (yamín) = right; the ending ה means "toward": ימינה = rightward (like הביתה = homeward). בצד ימין = on the right.

ex.en: At the end of the street, turn left.

note: Here ש is pronounced s: שמאל (smol) = left, שמאלה (smóla) = to the left, בצד שמאל = on the left.

ex.en: Keep going straight until the traffic light.

note: As an adjective it means straight or honest: בחורה ישרה = an honest young woman. Colloquially also "directly": אני הולך ישר הביתה = I'm going straight home.

ex.en: I live near the sea.

note: Also על יד (same meaning). With endings: לידי (next to me), לידך, לידו, לידה.

ex.en: The café is opposite the park.

note: With endings: מולי (opposite me), מולך, מולו, מולה. Also "against" in sport: מכבי מול הפועל.

ex.en: Our house is between the bank and the supermarket.

note: Two patterns: בין X ל-Y (most common) or בין X ובין Y. ביני לבינך = between you and me.

ex.en: The parking lot is behind the building.

note: Without a noun after it, say מאחור (me'akhór) = at the back. The opposite is לפני (in front of).

ex.en: The bank isn't far from here.

note: Feminine רחוקה, plural רחוקים / רחוקות. Far from = רחוק מ...; זה רחוק? = is it far?

ex.en: The supermarket is close, right on the corner.

note: Feminine קרובה. Close to = קרוב ל...: קרוב לבית = close to home. As a noun, קרוב משפחה = a relative.

ex.en: There's a café on the corner.

note: בפינה = on (or in) the corner. פינת אוכל = a dining area in an apartment.

ex.en: The supermarket is open until ten at night.

note: Short for סופרמרקט, and what everyone says. Careful: the same letters also spell סופר (sofér) = writer.

ex.en: I live in a tall building.

note: Root ב.נ.ה (to build). It's also the grammar word binyan, a verb pattern (pa'al, pi'el…).

ex.en: My office is in the city center.

note: מרכז העיר = downtown. המרכז on its own often means central Israel (the Tel Aviv area). מרכז מסחרי = a shopping center.

ex.en: The shop is closed on Shabbat.

note: Feminine, with an irregular plural: חנויות (khanuyót). חנות בגדים = a clothes shop.

ex.en: There's a small grocery store opposite the house.

note: The little neighbourhood grocery, as opposed to the big סופר. Feminine: מכולת קטנה.

ex.he: הילדים לא חוצים את הכביש לבד.
ex.en: The kids don't cross the road alone.

note: The road surface cars drive on; a רחוב is a street with houses and shops. Highways have numbers: כביש 1 links Tel Aviv and Jerusalem.

ex.en: You're not allowed to park on the sidewalk.

note: Same root as דרך (way, road).

ex.en: We crossed the bridge and turned right.

note: גשר להולכי רגל = a footbridge.

ex.en: Do you have a map of the city?

note: Also means a tablecloth: מפה לבנה על השולחן = a white tablecloth on the table.

ex.en: The police station is next to city hall.

note: Singular and feminine: המשטרה אומרת = the police say. A police officer is שוטר / שוטרת. The police phone number in Israel is 100.

ex.en: It's a very beautiful place.

note: Masculine, but the plural ends in -ot: מקומות (mekomót). Also "room, space": יש מקום? = is there room? / is this seat free?

ex.en: Excuse me, how do I get to the beach?

note: Lit. "how does one get to". No pronoun is needed: this impersonal plural is the normal way to ask for directions.

ex.en: The bank is on the other side of the street.

note: Irregular plural צדדים (tsdadím). בצד ימין / בצד שמאל = on the right / on the left.

ex.en: Is there an ATM near the supermarket?

note: A blend of כסף (money) + automat. To withdraw cash = למשוך כסף.

ex.en: My daughter dances at the community center.

note: Short for מרכז תרבות, נוער וספורט (center for culture, youth and sport): the neighbourhood center with after-school classes (חוגים) for kids and adults.

ex.en: I'm at home now.

note: Irregular plural בתים (batím). בבית = at home; הביתה = (to) home: אני הולכת הביתה. Before another noun it becomes בית (beit): בית ספר, בית קפה.

ex.en: My room is small but pleasant.

note: Plural חדרים (khadarím). Before another noun: חדר (khadar), as in חדר שינה, חדר ישיבות.

ex.en: We watch TV in the living room.

note: Israelis count the סלון as a room: a three-room apartment has a living room and two bedrooms. Not a hair salon (that's a מספרה).

ex.en: Dad is cooking in the kitchen.

note: Also "cuisine": המטבח הישראלי = Israeli cuisine. מטבח פתוח = an open-plan kitchen.

ex.he: יש לנו חדר שינה גדול עם מרפסת.
ex.en: We have a big bedroom with a balcony.

note: Lit. "room of sleep" (שינה = sleep). With "the": חדר השינה.

ex.en: Excuse me, is the toilet free?

note: Always plural, even for one toilet, so adjectives are plural too: השירותים פנויים. The polite word in Israel; it also means "services".

ex.he: המקלחת קטנה, אבל יש מים חמים.
ex.en: The shower is small, but there's hot water.

note: Both the shower and the room with it; many Israeli apartments have a shower, not a bathtub (אמבטיה). להתקלח = to take a shower.

ex.en: In the evening we sit on the balcony.

note: Most Israeli apartments have one. מרפסת שירות = a small utility balcony for laundry.

ex.en: The bed is new and comfortable.

note: מיטה זוגית = a double bed. To make the bed = לסדר את המיטה.

ex.en: The books are on the table.

note: Masculine, but the plural ends in -ot: שולחנות (shulkhanót). שולחן עבודה = a desk.

ex.en: Is there a free chair here?

note: Masculine, but the plural ends in -ot: כיסאות (kis'ót). Also spelled כסא.

ex.en: The clothes are in the closet.

note: Plural ארונות (-ot). ארון בגדים = a wardrobe; ארון מטבח = a kitchen cabinet.

ex.en: The cat is sleeping on the sofa.

note: ספה נפתחת = a sofa bed (lit. "a sofa that opens").

ex.en: The milk is in the fridge.

note: Same root as קר (cold): the thing that makes cold.

ex.en: The cake is in the oven.

note: Also a space heater: תנור חימום. The stovetop (hob) is called כיריים.

ex.en: Can I open the window?

note: Masculine, but the plural ends in -ot: חלונות (khalonót).

ex.en: The door is open.

note: Feminine (the -et ending): דלת פתוחה. Plural דלתות (dlatót).

ex.en: There's a beautiful picture on the wall.

note: Masculine, but the plural ends in -ot: קירות (kirót). An inside wall; a stone or city wall is a חומה.

ex.en: We live on the third floor.

note: Feminine, so the ordinal is feminine too: קומה שלישית. The ground floor is קומת קרקע, and קומה ראשונה is the floor above it.

ex.he: המעלית לא עובדת, אז אנחנו עולים במדרגות.
ex.en: The elevator isn't working, so we're taking the stairs.

note: The singular מדרגה (madregá) is one step. חדר מדרגות = the stairwell.

ex.he: אני צריכה מנורה חדשה לחדר השינה.
ex.en: I need a new lamp for the bedroom.

note: Any lamp, and also the seven-branched menorah on the emblem of the State of Israel. The Hanukkah lamp is a חנוכייה.

ex.en: The shoes are under the bed.

note: Usually with ל joined to the next word: מתחת לשולחן = under the table. Opposite: מעל (above). Without a noun: למטה (downstairs, down).

ex.en: There's a lamp above the table.

note: Also "more than": מעל מאה איש = over a hundred people. Opposite: מתחת ל. Without a noun: למעלה (upstairs, up).

ex.en: The food here is very tasty.

note: Same root as לאכול (to eat). Spelled like the verb form אוכל (okhél), as in אני אוכל = I eat; context tells you which.

ex.en: I buy bread every morning.

note: לחם מלא = wholewheat bread. On Shabbat many families eat חלה (challah).

ex.en: I drink coffee with milk.

note: מוצרי חלב = dairy products. חלב סויה, חלב שקדים = soy milk, almond milk.

ex.en: In the morning I eat two eggs.

note: Feminine, but the plural ends in -im: ביצים (beitsím), so numbers are feminine: שתי ביצים. ביצה קשה = a hard-boiled egg; חביתה = an omelette.

ex.en: I like bread with cheese.

note: גבינה לבנה = soft white cheese (a breakfast staple); גבינה צהובה = yellow (hard) cheese; קוטג׳ = cottage cheese.

ex.en: The tomatoes at the market are cheap today.

note: Also spelled עגבניה. עגבניות שרי = cherry tomatoes.

ex.en: I'm cutting a cucumber and a tomato for the salad.

note: מלפפון חמוץ = a pickle (lit. "sour cucumber").

ex.en: The girl is eating a green apple.

note: The full name is תפוח עץ ("tree apple"); תפוח אדמה ("earth apple") = potato.

ex.en: Are there any bananas at home?

note: Feminine (ends in ה): בננה צהובה.

ex.en: In the morning I drink orange juice.

note: Only the fruit: the colour orange is כתום. Orange juice uses the plural: מיץ תפוזים.

ex.en: There's rice and chicken for dinner.

note: A mass noun with no plural in normal use. מג׳דרה = rice (or bulgur) cooked with lentils.

ex.he: אני לא אוכל בשר, רק עוף ודגים.
ex.en: I don't eat meat, only chicken and fish.

note: Chicken on the plate; also bird or poultry in general. The live bird is a תרנגולת (hen) or תרנגול (rooster).

ex.en: On Friday we eat fish.

note: Both the animal and the food. Unlike English, Hebrew uses the plural for several fish: שני דגים.

ex.he: יש מסעדת בשר טובה ברחוב שלנו.
ex.en: There's a good meat restaurant on our street.

note: A mass noun. בשרי = meat (as a kosher category), the opposite of חלבי (dairy); kosher places serve one or the other.

ex.en: I buy vegetables at the market.

note: Mostly used in the plural: ירקות (yerakót). Same root as ירוק (green).

ex.en: In summer there's lots of fruit.

note: Irregular plural פירות (perót). Fruit and vegetables = פירות וירקות.

ex.en: In the morning I eat a vegetable salad.

note: סלט ישראלי = finely chopped tomato and cucumber. Also used for spreads and dips: restaurants often start with a table of סלטים.

ex.en: There's very good hummus here.

note: Both the dish and the chickpeas themselves. A חומוסייה is a small restaurant that serves mainly hummus.

ex.en: I'd like falafel in a pita.

note: Stress on the first syllable: píta. חצי פיתה = half a pita (a smaller portion).

ex.en: In summer I drink a lot of water.

note: Always plural and masculine: מים קרים = cold water, המים חמים = the water is hot. A glass of water = כוס מים.

ex.en: I'd like some juice, please.

note: מיץ סחוט = freshly squeezed juice; מיץ ענבים = grape juice.

ex.en: I drink tea with mint.

note: Tea with fresh mint (נענע) is very popular in Israel.

ex.en: Would you like coffee or tea?

note: Masculine, though it ends in ה: קפה חם. Popular orders: הפוך (a milky coffee, like a latte) and קפה שחור (Turkish-style black coffee). A café is a בית קפה.

ex.en: I drink coffee without sugar.

note: Stress on the last syllable: sukár. כמה סוכר? = how much sugar?

ex.en: It needs a bit more salt.

note: ים המלח = the Dead Sea (lit. "the Salt Sea").

ex.en: I cook with olive oil.

note: שמן זית = olive oil. Careful: the same letters spell the adjective שמן (shamén) = fat.

ex.en: What do you eat for breakfast?

note: Also ארוחת צהריים = lunch (for many Israelis the main meal) and ארוחת ערב = dinner. With "the": ארוחת הבוקר.

ex.en: Can I have another cup of coffee?

note: Feminine, though it has no feminine ending: כוס גדולה, שתי כוסות. Used for both a glass and a cup.
